Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 13, verse 1:

(p-180) Surat al-Ra'd is Medinan, though it has been said to be Meccan, except for His saying: ﴿And those who disbelieve say...﴾ to the end of the verse. It has forty-three verses.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Alif, Lam, Mim, Ra.﴾ It has been said that its meaning is: "I am Allah, the All-Knowing, the All-Seeing." ﴿These are the verses of the Book.﴾ By "the Book" is meant the surah, and "these" points to its verses, i.e., these verses are the verses of the complete surah, or of the Qur'an. ﴿And that which has been sent down to you from your Lord﴾ is the whole Qur'an. Its place in grammar is genitive, by conjunction with ﴿the Book﴾, in which case the general is conjoined to the particular, or one of the two descriptions is conjoined to the other. Or it is nominative, as a subject (mubtada'), with its predicate being ﴿the truth﴾, and the sentence then serves as a proof for the first sentence. The definiteness of the predicate, although it indicates that what is sent down is restricted to being the truth, is more general than what is sent down explicitly or implicitly, such as what is established by analogy (qiyas) and other things that the revelation has affirmed the goodness of following. ﴿But most people do not believe﴾, because of their neglect of reflection and contemplation upon it.

Allah is He who raised the heavens without pillars that you can see. (Note: translating the text as given.)

Wait, I should translate the passage faithfully and fully. Here is the complete translation:

﴿Allah is He who raised the heavens﴾ is a subject and predicate (mubtada' and khabar). It is permissible for the relative pronoun (al-mawsul) to be a qualifying description (sifah), with the predicate being ﴿He arranges the affair﴾.

﴿Without pillars﴾: asatin, the plural of 'imad (pillar), like ihab and ahab; or of 'amud, like adim and udum. It has also been read as ʿumud, like rusul.

﴿That you see﴾ is a qualifying description of ﴿pillars﴾, or a resumptive clause (isti'naf) serving as evidence by their seeing the heavens thus. This is a proof of the existence of the Wise Creator (al-Sani' al-Hakim), for their elevation above the other celestial bodies is, in the reality of being a physical body (al-jirmiyyah), and their being singled out with what necessitates that, must have a specifier that is neither a body nor corporeal, which prefers some of the possible things over others by His will. Upon this method is the rest of the signs mentioned.

﴿Then He established Himself over the Throne﴾ by preserving and governing.

﴿And He subjected the sun and the moon﴾ made them subservient to what He willed from them, such as their continuous motion at a certain speed that contributes to the coming-into-being and continuance of created things.

﴿Each runs for a specified term﴾ for a determined period in which their revolutions are completed, or toward a set end at which their course ceases, which is ﴿when the sun is wound up﴾ and ﴿when the stars fall and scatter﴾.

﴿He arranges the affair﴾: the affair of His dominion, of bringing into existence, annihilating, giving life, causing death, and other things.

﴿He details the signs﴾: He sends them down and makes them clear in detail, or He brings forth proofs one after another.

﴿That you may be certain of the meeting with your Lord﴾: so that you may reflect upon them and realize the perfection of His power, and thus know that He who is able to create these things and arrange them is able to restore and to recompense.

(p-181) ﴿And it is He who spread out the earth﴾: He extended it in length and breadth so that feet could firmly rest upon it and animals could move about on it. ﴿And placed upon it firm mountains﴾: mountains that are fixed, from rasa (ras'a), meaning a thing became stable when it settled; rawasi is the plural of rasiyah, and the ta' is for the feminine, either because it is an adjective of jibal (mountains) or for emphasis (mubalaghah).

﴿And rivers﴾: He joined them with the mountains and governed them with a single verb, inasmuch as the mountains are causes for the generation of rivers. ﴿And of all fruits﴾ is connected to His saying ﴿He placed therein two mates, two (kinds)﴾: that is, He placed in it, from all kinds of fruits, two varieties, such as sweet and sour, black and white, small and large. ﴿He covers the night with the day﴾: He clothes it in its place, so the atmosphere becomes dark after having been bright. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Abu Bakr recited ﴿yughshi﴾ with the doubled (shaddah) form.

﴿Indeed in that are signs for a people who reflect﴾ upon them. For their coming into being and their being specified in one respect rather than another is evidence of the existence of a wise Creator who ordered their affairs and prepared their causes.

﴿And in the earth are adjoining tracts﴾: some of them are good, some salty (sabakhah), some soft, some hard, and some suitable for crops but not for trees, and others the reverse. Were it not for the specification of a capable agent who brings about His actions in one manner rather than another, they would not be like this, since those tracts share the earthly nature and what necessarily follows from it and what befalls it through the mediation of celestial causes, inasmuch as they are contiguous and share in relations and conditions. ﴿And gardens of grapevines, and crops, and palm trees﴾: and orchards containing various kinds of trees and crops. The word "crops" (zar') is singular because it is originally a verbal noun (masdar). Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Ya'qub and Hafs recited ﴿wa-zar'un wa-nakhilun﴾ with the nominative (raf') as a conjunction upon ﴿jannat﴾. ﴿Sinwan﴾: palm trees sharing one root. ﴿Ghayru sinwan﴾: scattered ones of differing roots. Hafs recited with a damma (qinwan), which is the dialect of the Banu Tamim, like ﴿qinwan﴾ as the plural of qinw.

(They are watered with one water, and We favor some of them over others in fruit) in form, measure, scent and taste. This too is among the things that point to a wise Creator, for their difference while their roots and causes are uniform could only come about through the specification of a capable, choosing agent. Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim and Ya'qub recited yusqa with the masculine form, referring to what was mentioned; Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recited yufaddilu with the ya', to agree with His saying ﴿He regulates the affair﴾. ﴿Indeed in that are signs for a people who use their intellect﴾: who employ their minds through reflection.

"And if you are amazed [O Muhammad] at their denial of resurrection, then amazing is their saying: ﴿When we have become dust, shall we indeed be in a new creation?﴾" Their statement is truly worthy of being marvelled at, for whoever is able to originate what has been related to you, restoring it is the easiest thing for Him. The signs enumerated, just as they indicate the existence of the Originator, also indicate the possibility of resurrection, insofar as they show the perfection of His knowledge and power and the receptivity of matter to the varieties of His manipulation. ﴿When we have become dust, shall we indeed be in a new creation?﴾ is either a substitute for their saying or an object of a causative (maf'ul lahu), and the governing element of "idha" (when) is omitted, indicated by ﴿shall we indeed be in a new creation?﴾. ﴿Those are the ones who disbelieve in their Lord﴾, because they disbelieved in His power to resurrect. ﴿And those are the shackles around their necks﴾: they are bound by misguidance, their release is not hoped for, or they will be shackled on the Day of Resurrection. ﴿And those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever﴾, not separated from it. The placing of the separate pronoun (al-fasl, "those") serves to restrict eternal abiding to the disbelievers.

﴿They ask you to hasten the evil before the good﴾: that is, the punishment before well-being. They hastened what they were threatened with, namely the punishment of this world, mockingly. ﴿And exemplary punishments have already passed away before them﴾: the punishments of those like them among the deniers. Why then do they not take warning from them, and why do they not consider that the like of them could befall themselves? The word _al-mathulah_ (exemplary punishment), with a fatha or a damma on the tha', is like _al-sadaqah_ and _al-sudqah_, and it means punishment, because it is the like (_mithl_) of what the one punished deserved. From the same root comes _al-mithal_ for retaliation, and _amthaltu al-rajul min sahibihi_, meaning "I exacted retribution from him on behalf of his companion," when I make him pay for what he did. It was also read _al-mathulat_ with the tha' lightened, _al-muthulat_ with the fa' made to follow the ayn (i.e., the damma of the ayn applied to the fa'), and _al-muthulat_ with lightening after the following vowel. It was also read _al-mathalat_ with a fatha on the tha', as the plural of _mathalah_, like _rakabah_ and _rakabat_.

﴿And indeed your Lord is full of forgiveness for people despite their wrongdoing﴾: "despite their wrongdoing" means together with their wronging of themselves. Its position is accusative as a circumstantial clause (_hal_), and the element governing it is "forgiveness." Restricting the forgiveness in this way indicates that pardon before repentance is permissible, since the one who repents is no longer in his wrongdoing. Whoever prevents this restricts the wrongdoing to minor sins that are expiated for one who avoids major sins (_kaba'ir_), or interprets the forgiveness as concealment and granting of respite.

﴿And indeed your Lord is severe in punishment﴾: for the disbelievers, or for whomever He wills. It is reported from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Were it not for God's pardon and His overlooking, no one would have enjoyed life; and were it not for His threat and His punishment, everyone would have become complacent."

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 13, verse 7:

﴿And those who disbelieve say: "Why has no sign been sent down to him from his Lord?"﴾ (They say this) because they do not give weight to the signs sent down upon him, and as a demand for things like those given to Musa and Isa, upon them both be peace. ﴿You are only a warner﴾, a messenger sent for warning, like the other messengers before you, and it is not incumbent upon you except to bring what establishes your prophethood from the kind of miracles, not what they propose to you. ﴿And for every people there is a guide﴾: a prophet specifically endowed with miracles of the kind that predominates among them, who guides them to the truth and calls them to what is right; or (the meaning is) that Allah, exalted is He, is able to guide them, but He does not guide except whom He wills to be guided, by means of what He sends down to you of the signs. Then He followed that with what indicates the perfection of His knowledge and power and the comprehensiveness of His decree and destiny, as a reminder that He, exalted is He, is able to send down what they have proposed, but He did not send it down because He knows that their proposal is out of obstinacy and not seeking guidance; and that He is able to guide them, but He did not guide them because His decree of disbelief preceded. So He said:

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 13, verse 8:

﴿Allah knows what every female carries﴾, that is, her pregnancy, or what she carries in whatever state it is, of the states present and awaited. ﴿And what the wombs diminish and what they increase﴾, that is, what they lessen and what they increase in its form (jinnah), its duration and its number. The longest duration of pregnancy is four years according to us, five years according to Malik, and two years according to Abu Hanifa.

It is narrated that al-Dahhak was born after two years, and Harim ibn Hayyan after four years, and the highest number [of births] has no limit.

It is said that the limit of what is known [of this] is four, and Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, went to this view. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "A shaykh in Yemen told me that his wife gave birth in several deliveries, with five in each delivery." It is also said that what is meant is the decrease and increase of menstrual blood. Ghada (ghāḍa) came both transitively and intransitively, and likewise izdada. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿and they increased by nine﴾. If you make both of them intransitive, then it is necessary that [the verb] be taken as a verbal noun (maṣdariyyah). Their attribution to the wombs is metaphorical, since they belong to Allah the Exalted or to what is in them. ﴿And everything with Him is in measure﴾, by a measure that it neither exceeds nor falls short of, like His saying the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, We created everything with measure﴾. He, the Exalted, specified each occurrence with a particular time and state, and prepared for it causes leading to it that necessitate that.

Ibn Kathir read ﴿hādin﴾, ﴿wālin﴾, ﴿wāqin﴾, and ﴿wa-mā ʿinda Allāhi bāqin﴾ with tanwin when connected; when pausing, he pauses with a yā' in these four words wherever they occur, and no others. The rest connect with tanwin and pause without a yā'.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 13, verses 9–10:

﴿ʿĀlimu l-ghayb﴾ (He who knows the unseen), the absent from the senses. ﴿Wa sh-shahādah﴾ (and the witnessed), the present to them. ﴿Al-Kabīr﴾ (the Great), the one of great majesty, from whose knowledge nothing escapes. ﴿Al-Mutaʿāl﴾ (the Exalted), the one who is elevated above everything by His power; or the one who is too great to be described by the attributes of created beings, and is exalted above them.

﴿Sawāʾun minkum man asarra l-qawl﴾ (It is the same among you whoever conceals speech) within himself, ﴿wa man jahara bihi﴾ (and whoever speaks it aloud) to another. ﴿Wa man huwa mustakhfin bi l-layl﴾ (and whoever hides himself by night), seeking concealment in a hiding place at night. ﴿Wa sāribun﴾ (and one who goes forth), manifest, ﴿bi n-nahār﴾ (by day), seen by everyone; from sariba, surūban, meaning he came out into the open. This is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) upon "man" or upon "mustakhfin," on the basis that "man" carries the sense of the dual, as in the verse:

"Let us be like the one who, O wolf, keeps company" (nakun mithla man yā dhi'bu yaṣṭaḥibān)

As if he said: "It is the same among you, two persons: one who hides himself by night, and one who goes forth by day." The verse is connected to what precedes it, establishing the perfection and comprehensiveness of His knowledge.

As if he said: "It is the same among you, two persons: one who hides himself by night, and one who goes forth by day." The verse is connected to what precedes it, establishing the perfection and comprehensiveness of His knowledge.

**﴿For him﴾**: for whoever keeps his speech secret or speaks aloud, or hides himself or goes about openly (*sariba*).

**﴿Mu'aqqibat﴾** (angels who follow one another in succession): angels who take turns in guarding him. It is the plural of *mu'aqqibah*, from *'aqqabahu*, an intensive form of *'aqabahu*, meaning "he came after him, following on his heels," as though some of them follow others. Or it is because they follow up his words and deeds and record them. Or it comes from *i'taqaba*, with the *ta'* assimilated into the *qaf* (giving *mu'aqqibat*), and the *ta'* is for emphasis. Or the intended meaning of *al-mu'aqqibat* is groups.

It is also read as *Ma'aqib* (*ma'aqib*), the plural of *mu'aqqib* or *mu'aqqibah*, with a *ya'* substituted for the omitted one of the two *qaf*s.

**﴿From before him and from behind him﴾**: from his sides. Or, from among his deeds, what has been put forward and what has been put back.

**﴿They guard him from the command of God﴾**: from His punishment, whenever he sins, by granting him respite or by asking forgiveness for him. Or they guard him from harms, or they watch over his affairs by the command of God, exalted is He. This has also been read so. It is said that *min* here means *bi* (by/through). It is also said that *min amri Allah* is a second attributive description of **﴿mu'aqqibat﴾**.

It is said that *al-mu'aqqibat* are the guards and the *jalawizah* (police/enforcers) around the ruler, who protect him, in his imagination, from the decree of God, exalted is He.

**﴿Indeed God does not change what is with a people﴾**: of well-being and blessing.

**﴿until they change what is in themselves﴾**: of good states, to ugly states.

**﴿And when God wills evil for a people, there is no turning it back﴾**: there is no one to repel it. The governing element in *idha* (when) is what the answer (*jawab*) indicates.

**﴿And they have no protector other than Him﴾**: none among those who manage their affairs and who would ward off evil from them. In this is evidence that opposing the will of God, exalted is He, is impossible.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 13, verses 12–13:

﴿He it is who shows you the lightning, [causing] fear [of its harm]﴾ and ﴿hope [of rain]﴾. The two words ﴿fear﴾ and ﴿hope﴾ are in the accusative of cause (ʿillah), with an omitted noun: i.e., [He shows it for] the desire (irādah) of fear and hope; or they are interpreted as ﴿causing fear and causing hope﴾; or they are a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring to ﴿the lightning﴾ or to the addressees, with a dhū understood; or the verbal noun is used in the sense of the passive or active participle for emphasis. It is said: whoever would be harmed by the rain fears it, and whoever would benefit from it hopes for it.

﴿And He produces the clouds﴾, the heavy clouds drawn along in the air. ﴿Heavy﴾ is the plural of thaqilah, and the cloud is described by it because it is a collective noun in the sense of a plural.

﴿And the thunder glorifies [Him]﴾, and those who hear it glorify [Him]. ﴿With His praise﴾, being accompanied by it, so they cry out "Glory be to God" and "Praise be to God." Or, the thunder itself, by its very nature, indicates the oneness of God and the perfection of His power, accompanied by an indication of His grace and the descent of His mercy.

It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with them both, that the Prophet (ﷺ) was asked about thunder, and he said: "It is an angel appointed over the clouds, with whips of fire with which he drives the clouds."

﴿And the angels [glorify Him] out of fear of Him﴾, out of fear of God the Exalted and reverence for Him. It is said the pronoun refers to ﴿the thunder﴾. ﴿And He sends the thunderbolts and strikes with them whom He wills﴾, destroying him. ﴿Yet they dispute about God﴾, in that they deny the Messenger of God (ﷺ) regarding what he describes Him with of perfect knowledge, power, sole divinity, and the resurrection and recompense of people. Jidal (disputation) is excessive strictness in contention, from jadl, which means twisting; the waw is either coordinating one sentence with another or indicates a circumstantial clause. For it is narrated that ʿAmir ibn al-Tufayl and Arbad ibn Rabiʿah, brother of Labid, came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) intending to kill him. ʿAmir engaged him in argument, while Arbad circled behind him to strike him with the sword. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) noticed this and said: "O God, suffice me against them both by whatever You will." So God sent a thunderbolt upon Arbad, which killed him, and struck ʿAmir with a tumor, and he died in the house of a woman of Salul. He used to say: "A tumor like the tumor of a camel, and death in the house of a woman of Salul." So this verse was revealed.

﴿And He is severe in might﴾. Al-mimahalah means plotting against His enemies, from mahala fulan bi-fulan when he plotted against him and exposed him to destruction; and from it comes tamahhala, when one takes pains to employ cunning. Perhaps its root is al-mahl in the sense of drought. It is also said it is fa'al from al-mahl in the sense of strength. It is also said it is mufʿil from al-hawl or al-hilah, irregularly made into a weak (ʿilal) form; supporting this is that it is read with a fatha on the mim, as mufʿal from ḥāla yaḥūlu, meaning to devise. It may also mean "the spine," so it would be a metaphor for strength and power, like their saying: "the forearm of God is stronger and His razor sharper."

**Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 13, verse 14:**

﴿To Him is the true call﴾ The true supplication (al-du'a al-haqq): for He is the One who truly deserves to be worshipped and to be called upon to worship, to the exclusion of anything else. Or, "to Him is the answered call," for whoever calls upon Him, He answers him. This is supported by what follows it. And "the true" (al-haqq), on both readings, is that which contradicts falsehood (al-batil). The idafa (annexation) of "call" (da'wa) to it is because of the connection between them (mulabasa), or it is understood as "the call of the one called upon is true." It has been said that al-Haqq is God Most High, and every call to Him is "the call of the Truth." As for what is meant by the two clauses: if the verse is about Arbad and Amir, then their destruction from a direction they did not perceive is a sign from God answering the call of His Messenger (ﷺ), or an indication that he was upon the truth. If the verse is general, then what is meant is a warning to the disbelievers for disputing with the Messenger of God (ﷺ), by the descent of the calamity upon them and a threat of the answering of the Messenger's (ﷺ) supplication against them, or a clarification of their error and the corruption of their opinion. ﴿And those who call upon﴾, that is, and the idols which the polytheists call upon; the returning pronoun has been omitted. Or, and the polytheists who call upon idols; the object has been omitted, the indication of it being ﴿besides Him﴾. ﴿They do not answer them with anything﴾ of their requests. ﴿Except as one who stretches out his hands﴾ except with a response like the response of one who spreads his hands ﴿toward the water so that it may reach his mouth﴾, asking it to reach him. ﴿But it will not reach it﴾, because it is an inanimate thing that neither perceives his supplication nor is able to answer him; and bringing about what is other than that for which it was created applies likewise to their gods. It has been said that they are likened, in the scantiness of the benefit of their calling upon them, to one who wishes to scoop up water to drink it, so he spreads his hands to drink. It is also read ﴿tad'una﴾ with the ta', and ﴿basit﴾ with tanwin. ﴿And the supplication of the disbelievers is only in error﴾, in loss, ruin and falsehood.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 13, verse 15:

﴿And to Allah prostrate whoever is in the heavens and the earth, willingly and unwillingly﴾. It is possible that the prostration (al-sujud) is in its literal sense, for the angels and the believers among the two species (humans and jinn) prostrate to Him, willingly, in both states of hardship and ease, while the disbelievers prostrate unwillingly, in the state of hardship and necessity.

﴿And their shadows﴾ by extension (bi-al-'ard). It may also be that what is meant is their submission (inqiyad) to the bringing about of what He wills of them, whether they wish it or dislike it, and the submission of their shadows to His directing of them by lengthening and shortening. The accusative of ﴿willingly and unwillingly﴾ is as a circumstantial qualifier (al-hal) or as a reason clause (al-'illa). His saying: ﴿in the mornings and the evenings﴾ is an adverbial complement (zarf) of ﴿prostrate﴾, and what is meant by the two is continuity, or it is a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of the shadows. The specifying of the two times is because shadows become largest and most numerous in them. Al-Ghuduw (mornings) is the plural of ghadah (morning), like qina the plural of qanah (reed). And al-Asal (evenings) is the plural of asil, which is the period between the afternoon prayer ('asr) and the sunset (maghrib). It has been said that al-ghuduw is a verbal noun (masdar), and what supports this is that it has also been read as al-iSal (wa al-'iyṣal), which is entering the time of asil.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 13, verse 16:

﴿Say: "Who is the Lord of the heavens and the earth?"﴾, meaning: their Creator and the one who manages their affairs. ﴿Say: "Allah."﴾ Answer them with this, since they have no answer other than it, and because it is the clear truth which cannot be disputed. Or prompt them to give this answer. ﴿Say: "Have you then taken, besides Him, protectors who possess no power to benefit or harm even themselves?"﴾ Then compel them with this, because their taking such protectors is a denial far removed from the demands of reason. ﴿Protectors who possess no power to benefit or harm even themselves﴾ means they cannot bring benefit to themselves or ward off harm from themselves. How then could they be able to bring benefit to others or ward off harm from them? This is a second proof of their misguidance and the corruption of their opinion in taking protectors, hoping that they would intercede for them. ﴿Say: "Are the blind and the seeing equal?"﴾ The blind is the polytheist, ignorant of the reality of worship and of what makes it obligatory, and the seeing is the monotheist who knows this. It was also said: the blind is the worshipped one who is unaware of you, and the seeing is the worshipped one who observes your conditions. ﴿Or are the darknesses and the light equal?﴾ The darknesses are polytheism and the light is monotheism. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Abu Bakr read it with the yā' (ي). ﴿Or have they set up for Allah partners who created as He creates, so that the creation seemed alike to them?﴾ Rather, did they set them up, with the hamza (أ) being interrogative of denial? His saying ﴿who created as He creates﴾ is a description of "partners," falling under the same denial.

﴿So that the creation seemed alike to them﴾ means: the creation of Allah and their creation. The meaning is that they did not take for Allah partners who create like Him, such that the creation would appear alike to them, so that they would say, "These have created as Allah created, and so they deserve worship as He deserves it." Rather, they took as partners beings that are powerless, who cannot do what even created beings can do, let alone what the Creator can do. ﴿Say: "Allah is the Creator of everything."﴾ That is, there is no creator other than Him, so that He would have a sharer in worship. He made creation the requirement of worship and the necessary condition for deserving it, and then negated it from anyone other than Him, so as to indicate His saying: ﴿And He is the One,﴾ who is singular in divinity. ﴿The Subduer,﴾ who prevails over everything.

Revealed from the sky, water: from the clouds, or from the direction of the sky, or from the sky itself, since the beginnings of it are from there.

﴿So the valleys flowed﴾ with rivers. It is the plural of *wadi* (valley), which is the place where water flows abundantly; the word was then extended and applied to the water flowing in it. It is indefinite because rain falls in alternation among the lands. ﴿According to their measure﴾ according to the quantity that God, exalted is He, knew to be beneficial and not harmful, or according to their measure in smallness and greatness. ﴿The torrent carried a foam﴾ it lifted it up, and *zabad* (foam) is the scum of boiling. ﴿Mounting﴾ high. (And from what they kindle upon the fire) it covers the metals such as gold, silver, iron and copper, in a manner of disregard for them, to show His majesty.

﴿Seeking an ornament﴾ that is, seeking an adornment. ﴿Or goods﴾ such as utensils and instruments of war and tillage. The purpose of this is to explain their benefits. ﴿There is a foam like it﴾ that is, and from what they kindle upon it there is a foam like the foam of the water, which is its dross. The *min* (from) is for the beginning or for partition. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Hafs read it with the *ya'* (third person), on the basis that the pronoun refers to the people, and its being omitted is due to knowledge of it. ﴿Thus God strikes the truth and falsehood﴾ the likeness of truth and falsehood. For truth is like the water that descends from the sky, so the valleys flow with it according to need and benefit, and various kinds of benefit are gained from it; and it remains in the earth, in that part of it settles in its places of benefit and part of it travels through the veins of the earth to springs, wells and boreholes. And truth is like the metal that is benefited from in forging ornaments and making various goods, and that lasts for a long period. Falsehood is like its foam, in the scarcity of its benefit and the swiftness of its passing away. He explained this by His saying: ﴿As for the foam, it departs as scum﴾ it is swept away by it, that is, the torrent casts it away; and the molten metal. Its accusative is as a circumstantial state. It is also read *jufalan*, and the meaning is the same. ﴿As for that which benefits people﴾ such as water and the pure part of the metal. ﴿It remains in the earth﴾ its people benefit from it. ﴿Thus God strikes the parables﴾ to clarify the ambiguous matters.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 13, verse 18:

﴿For those who respond to their Lord, there is the best (reward).﴾ "Those who respond" refers to the believers who responded. ﴿For their Lord, the best (reward)﴾: the response is the best (response).

﴿But those who do not respond to Him﴾: they are the disbelievers. The lam (in "li-") is connected to yadribu (He strikes/sets forth), on the basis that He made the setting forth of the parable a matter concerning the two groups, i.e., the setting forth of the parable for both of them.

It has also been said that ﴿lilladhina istajabu﴾ ("for those who responded") is the predicate of al-husna (the best), which is the reward (al-mathubah) or the Garden (al-Jannah). And ﴿wa-alladhina lam yastajibu﴾ ("but those who did not respond") is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is:

﴿Had they everything that is on the earth, all of it, and the like of it with it, they would surely ransom themselves with it.﴾ According to the first view, this is an independent statement (kalam mubtada') explaining the final state of those who did not respond.

﴿Those—for them is the evil of the reckoning﴾: and this is the scrutiny of it, that a man is held to account for his sin and nothing of it is forgiven.

﴿And their abode is﴾: their place of return (marji'uhum).

﴿Hell; and wretched is the resting-place (al-mihad)﴾: al-mihad is the place of settling (al-musta arr), and the object of blame (al-makhsus bil-dhamm) is omitted.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 13, verses 19–20:

﴿Is he who knows that what has been sent down to you from your Lord is the truth﴾ [equal to] one who is blind? ﴿Blind﴾ means blind of heart, who gains no insight and so does not respond. The hamza (interrogative particle) here is for denying that there could be any doubt about their being alike, after the parable has been struck. ﴿Only those of understanding remember﴾, i.e. the people of intellect (dhawu al-'uqul), whose minds are free from following mere assumption and opposing illusion.

﴿Those who fulfil the covenant of Allah﴾: that which they bound upon themselves of acknowledging His lordship when they said "Yes" (bala), or that which Allah the Exalted enjoined upon them in His books. ﴿And do not break the solemn pact﴾: that which they confirmed of covenants between themselves and Allah the Exalted, and between themselves and the servants; and this is a generalisation after a specification (ta'mim ba'da takhsis).

Those who join what God has commanded to be joined (﴿والَّذِينَ يَصِلُونَ ما أمَرَ اللَّهُ بِهِ أنْ يُوصَلَ﴾), from the ties of kinship, allegiance to the believers, and belief in all the prophets, upon them be peace; and included in this is observing all the rights of people. And they fear their Lord (﴿وَيَخْشَوْنَ رَبَّهُمْ﴾), His threat, in general. And they dread the evil of the reckoning (﴿وَيَخافُونَ سُوءَ الحِسابِ﴾), in particular, so they take account of themselves before they are called to account.

Those who are patient (﴿والَّذِينَ صَبَرُوا﴾) in what the self dislikes and what desire opposes. Seeking the face of their Lord (﴿ابْتِغاءَ وجْهِ رَبِّهِمْ﴾), desiring His pleasure, not for reward, reputation or the like. And they establish the prayer (﴿وَأقامُوا الصَّلاةَ﴾), the obligatory prayer. And they spend from what We have provided them (﴿وَأنْفَقُوا مِمّا رَزَقْناهُمْ﴾), some of it, that which it is obligatory for them to spend.

Secretly (﴿سِرًّا﴾) for one who is not known for wealth, and openly (﴿وَعَلانِيَةً﴾) for one who is known for it. And they repel evil with good (﴿وَيَدْرَءُونَ بِالحَسَنَةِ السَّيِّئَةَ﴾), repelling it with it, so they repay wrongdoing with kindness, or they follow an evil deed with a good one that erases it. For them is the good end of the abode (﴿أُولَئِكَ لَهم عُقْبى الدّارِ﴾), the outcome of the world, and what the end of its people ought to be, which is Paradise. The sentence is the predicate of the relative pronouns (mawsul) if they are taken as the subject through the inchoative, and if they are made attributes of "those of understanding," then it is a resumptive sentence (istinaf) mentioning what they deserve through those attributes.

﴿Jannāt ʿAdnin﴾ is either a substitute (badal, an apposition) for ﴿ʿUqbā al-Dār﴾, or a subject (mubtadaʾ, nominal subject) whose predicate (khabar, the predicate) is ﴿yadkhulūnahā﴾. ʿAdn means settled residence, so the meaning is "gardens in which they will dwell." It was also said that it is the innermost part of Paradise (buṭnān al-jannah).

﴿Wa-man ṣalaḥa min ābāʾihim wa-azwājihim wa-dhurriyyātihim﴾ is coordinated (ʿaṭf, conjunction) with the nominative pronoun in ﴿yadkhulūna﴾. The separation was made acceptable by the other pronoun. Alternatively, it is an object of accompaniment (mafʿūl maʿahu, object of accompaniment). The meaning is that whoever among their families is righteous will be joined to them, even if he does not reach their rank of excellence, as a follower of them and as an honour to their station. This is evidence that the rank is raised through intercession. Or it means that those described by these attributes are grouped with one another, because of the kinship and ties between them in entering Paradise, for greater companionship. Restricting it to righteousness indicates that mere lineage does not benefit.

﴿Wal-malāʾikatu yadkhulūna ʿalayhim min kulli bāb﴾: from the gates of the abodes, or from the gates of victories and gifts, saying:

﴿Salāmun ʿalaykum﴾ is good news of the continuance of safety. ﴿Bimā ṣabartum﴾ is connected either to ﴿ʿalaykum﴾, or to an implied element, meaning "this is because of what you endured," not to ﴿salāmun﴾, since the predicate would then be separated. The bāʾ (preposition) is causal (sababiyyah, indicating cause) or substitutive (badaliyyah, indicating exchange). ﴿Fa-niʿma ʿuqbā al-Dār﴾. It is also read as ﴿fa-naʿma﴾ with a fatḥah on the nūn (n). The original form is niʿma, and the ʿayn was made sukūn by transferring its kasrah to the fāʾ, and other forms are also possible. (p-187)

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 13, verse 25:

﴿And those who break the covenant of Allah﴾ meaning: the opposites of the former ones. ﴿after its pledge﴾ after they had bound themselves to it through acknowledgment and acceptance. ﴿and sever what Allah has commanded to be joined﴾ and ﴿cause corruption on the earth﴾ through wrongdoing and the stirring up of strife. ﴿For them is the curse, and for them is the evil abode﴾: the punishment of Jahannam (Hell), or the evil outcome of this world, since it stands in contrast to ʿUqba al-Dar (the good final abode).

Allah extends provision to whomever He wills and restricts it. (Allah) expands it for whom He wills and constricts it for whom He wills.

﴿And they rejoice in the worldly life﴾: i.e., the people of Makkah, rejoicing in what was extended to them in this world.

﴿Yet the worldly life, in comparison to the Hereafter, is nothing but a fleeting enjoyment﴾: i.e., in comparison to the Hereafter. ﴿Is but a fleeting enjoyment﴾: an enjoyment that does not last, like the brief provision of a rider or the food of a shepherd. The meaning is that they became exultant over what they gained of the world, did not spend it on that which would earn them the bliss of the Hereafter, and were deceived by what, in comparison to it, is a meager thing of little benefit and swift to vanish.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 13, verses 27–29:

﴿And those who disbelieve say: "Why has not a sign been sent down upon him from his Lord?" Say: "Indeed, Allah leaves astray whom He wills"﴾ by proposing signs after the miracles have become manifest. ﴿And guides to Himself whoever turns penitently﴾ — who turns to the truth and gives up obstinacy. This is a reply that serves as an expression of wonder at their statement, as if he said: "Say to them: how great is your obstinacy! Indeed, Allah leaves astray whoever He wills from among those who share your attributes, so there is no way for them to be guided even if I send down every sign." ﴿And guides to Himself whoever turns penitently﴾ — by what I have brought, indeed by something less than it of the signs.

﴿Those who believe﴾ is either a substitute for ﴿whoever﴾ or the predicate of an omitted subject. ﴿And their hearts find rest in the remembrance of Allah﴾ — finding comfort in Him, relying upon Him, and hoping from Him; or, in the remembrance of His mercy after anxiety over fear of Him; or, in the remembrance of His proofs that indicate His existence and His oneness; or, in His speech, meaning the Qur'an, which is the greatest of the miracles. ﴿Verily, in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest﴾ — they become tranquil through it.

﴿Those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ is the subject, whose predicate is ﴿Tuba for them﴾. Ṭūbā (good fortune, blessedness) is of the form fu‘lā derived from al-ṭayyib (the good), its yā' changed to wāw because of the ḍammah preceding it; it is a verbal noun from ṭāba (to be good), like Bushrā (good news) and Zulfā (nearness). It may be in the nominative or the accusative case, and for this reason it has been read as ﴿wa-ḥusna maʼāb﴾ (and a good return) in the accusative.

Thus (kadhalika): just as that, meaning the sending of messengers before you. "We have sent you to a community (ummah) before which other communities (umam) have passed away" means: other communities preceded it. "Communities" were sent to them, so your being sent to them is no novelty. "So that you might recite to them that which We have revealed to you" means: so that you might read to them the Book which We have revealed to you. "And yet they disbelieve in the Most Merciful (al-Rahman)" means: and their state is that they disbelieve in the One of intense mercy (al-Baligh al-Rahmah), whose blessing encompasses them and whose mercy embraces everything. Yet they did not give thanks for His blessings, especially what He bestowed upon them by sending you to them and sending down the Qur'an, which is the source of the religious and worldly benefits for them. It has been said that it was revealed concerning the polytheists of Makkah when it was said to them, "Prostrate yourselves to the Most Merciful," and they said, "And what is the Most Merciful?" "Say: He is my Lord" means: al-Rahman is my Creator and the one who manages my affairs. "There is no god but Him" means: none deserves worship besides Him.

(p-188) "Upon Him I have relied" means: in my victory over you. "And to Him is my return" (matab) means: my return and your return.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 13, verse 31:

﴿And if there were a Qur'an by which the mountains were set in motion﴾ is a conditional clause whose response has been omitted. Its purpose is either to magnify the status of the Qur'an, or to emphasise the obstinacy and stubbornness of the disbelievers. That is: "Even if there were a Book by which the mountains were uprooted from their places, or by which the earth were cut asunder, its clefts splitting out of fear of God at its recitation, or it were split so that rivers and springs gushed forth." ﴿Or by which the dead were made to speak﴾, so that they would hear and read it, or hear and respond when it is recited. It would still be this Qur'an, for it is the utmost in miraculousness and the ultimate in admonition and warning. Or [the response is]: "they would still not have believed in it," like His saying: ﴿And even if We had sent down to them the angels﴾, to the end of the verse.

It is said that the Quraysh said: "O Muhammad, if it would please you that we follow you, then set your Qur'an to move the mountains away from Makkah so that it becomes spacious for us, and we may make in it gardens and estates; or subject the wind to us by it so that we may ride it and trade to Syria; or raise for us by it Qusayy ibn Kilab and our other forefathers so that they may speak with us about you." So it was revealed. On this view, "cutting the earth" means cutting it through by travel.

It is also said that the response comes first, and it is His saying: ﴿while they disbelieve in the Most Merciful﴾, and what lies between them is a parenthetical interjection and a reminder. The word ﴿was spoken to﴾ is used specifically because the dead include a true rational being (i.e., the dead who are men).

﴿Rather, to God belongs the affair entirely﴾: rather, to God belongs the power over everything. This is a turning away from what the meaning of negation in "law" (law) implies. That is: rather, God is able to bring what they have demanded of the signs, but His will has not been directed toward that, knowing that their obstinacy would not yield to Him. This is supported by His saying: ﴿Have not those who believe despaired﴾ of their faith, despite what they have seen of their conditions. Most of them held that its meaning is "Have they not known," on the basis that ʿAli, Ibn ʿAbbas and a group of the Companions and Successors, may God be pleased with them all, read: "Have they not ascertained [yatabayyan]," and this is its explanation. The word "despair" (yaʾs) is used in the sense of knowledge because it is caused by knowledge, for what one despairs of can only be something known. For this reason it is connected to His saying: ﴿that, had God willed, He would have guided mankind entirely﴾, for its meaning is the negation of the guidance of some people, since the will has not been attached to their being guided. On the first view it is connected to an omitted element, the estimated sense being: "Have not those who believe despaired of their faith, knowing that, had God willed, He would have guided mankind entirely," or it is connected to ﴿believed﴾.

﴿And those who disbelieve will not cease to be struck by what they have wrought﴾ of disbelief and evil deeds. ﴿A calamity﴾: a disaster that strikes them and unsettles them. ﴿Or it descends close to their dwellings﴾, so that they are frightened by it and its sparks fly toward them. It is said that the verse concerns the disbelievers of Makkah, for they will not cease to be afflicted by what they did to the Messenger of God ﷺ, for he, upon whom be blessings and peace, would continually send raiding parties against them, which would attack around them and seize their livestock. On this view, it is permissible that ﴿descends﴾ is addressed to the Messenger, upon whom be blessings and peace, for he did descend with his army close to their dwellings in the year of al-Hudaybiyyah. ﴿Until the promise of God comes﴾: death, or the Resurrection, or the conquest of Makkah. ﴿Indeed God does not break the promise﴾, because lying is impossible in His speech.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 13, verse 32:

﴿And indeed, messengers before you were mocked, but I granted respite to those who disbelieved; then I seized them, and how was My punishment?﴾ It is a consolation to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and a warning to those who mocked him and to those who made demands upon him. Al-imlā' (granting respite) means that one is left for a span of time in ease and security. ﴿Then I seized them, and how was My punishment?﴾ That is, My punishment of them.

(p-189) ﴿Is then He who stands watching over every soul, [recording] what it has earned of good or of evil,﴾ and nothing of their deeds is hidden from Him, nor is anything of their recompense lost to Him, [equal to those who do not?]. The predicate is omitted, and its estimated form is: "like one who is not so."

﴿And they have set up partners for God﴾ is either a resumed sentence (istinaf) or a conjunction ('atf) upon ﴿earned﴾, if the particle "ma" is taken as a verbal particle (ma masdariyya). Or the meaning is: they did not affirm His oneness, and they set up partners, and the 'atf is upon that. Here the apparent noun (al-ẓahir) is used in place of the pronoun, to draw attention to the fact that He is the one who deserves worship. His words ﴿Say: name them﴾ are a reminder that these partners do not deserve it. The meaning is: describe them, and look whether they possess anything by which they deserve worship and are qualified for partnership.

﴿Or will you inform Him of what He does not know on earth?﴾ means: rather, do you inform Him? It is also read tunbi'unahu with takhfif (lightened pronunciation). ﴿Of what He does not know on earth﴾ means: partners who deserve worship, whom He does not know, or attributes by which they deserve it, which He does not know, while He is the Knower of everything.

﴿Or [do you name them] with an apparent utterance of speech?﴾ means: do you name them partners with a mere outward expression, without any reality or consideration of meaning, like naming the Zanji (African) "Kafur" (camphor). This is an eloquent argument in a wondrous style, which proclaims its own inimitability (i'jaz).

﴿Rather, their scheming has been made attractive to those who disbelieved﴾: their deception, so that they imagined falsehoods and then took them to be truth; or their plotting against Islam by their polytheism. ﴿And they were averted from the way﴾, the way of truth. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read (wa-ṣaddū) with a fatha, meaning: and they averted people from faith. It is also read with a kasra as "ṣiddun" with tanwin (nunation, the addition of a final "n" sound to indicate indefiniteness). ﴿And whomever God leaves astray﴾ means: forsakes him. ﴿For him there is no guide﴾ means: none who grants him success toward guidance.

﴿For them is a punishment in the life of this world﴾ by killing, capture, and all the other calamities that befall them. ﴿And the punishment of the Hereafter is harder﴾ because of its severity and its permanence. ﴿And they have no protector from God﴾, from His punishment or from His mercy, ﴿no defender﴾, no one to protect them.

﴿The parable of the Garden which the God-fearing have been promised﴾: its description, which is a parable in its strangeness. It is a *mubtada'* (subject of a nominal sentence) whose predicate (*khabar*) is omitted according to Sibawayh, meaning: "in what We have related to you is the parable of the Garden." It was said that its predicate is the following.

﴿Rivers flow beneath it﴾: this follows the pattern of your saying "صِفَةُ زَيْدٍ أسْمَرُ" (the attribute of Zayd is dark-complexioned), or it is by omitting a qualified noun, meaning "the parable of the Garden is a garden beneath which rivers flow," or by the addition of *al-mathal* (the parable), and this, according to Sibawayh's view, is a *hal* (circumstantial clause) either from the returning pronoun, or from the omitted element, or from the relative clause.

﴿Its fruit is constant﴾: its fruit does not cease.

﴿And its shade﴾: that is, and its shade (is constant). Likewise, it is not erased by the sun in this world. ﴿That﴾: that is, the described Garden.

﴿The final outcome of those who were God-fearing﴾: their ultimate destination and the end of their affair.

﴿And the final outcome of the disbelievers is the Fire﴾ alone and nothing else. In the arrangement of the two statements there is encouragement for the God-fearing and despair for the disbelievers.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 13, verse 36:

﴿Those to whom We gave the Book rejoice at what has been sent down to you﴾. He means the Muslims among the People of the Book, such as Ibn Salam (ʿAbdullah ibn Salam) and his companions, and those Christians who believed. They were eighty men: forty in Najran, eight in Yemen, and thirty-two in Abyssinia. Or, most of them, for they used to rejoice at whatever agreed with their scriptures. ﴿And among the factions﴾. He means their disbelievers, who formed factions against the Messenger of Allah ﷺ with enmity, such as Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf and his companions, and al-Sayyid and al-ʿAqib and their partisans. ﴿Some of them deny part of it﴾. This is what contradicts their laws, or what agrees with what they had distorted of them. ﴿Say: I have only been commanded to worship Allah and not associate anything with Him﴾. This is a reply to the deniers, meaning: say to them, "I have been commanded in what was sent down to me to worship Allah and to affirm His oneness, and this is the foundation of the religion, and you have no way to deny it. As for what you deny because it contradicts your laws, the contradiction of laws and divine books in particular rulings is no novelty." It has been read as "wa-lā ushriku" with a raised final vowel (rafʿ), as a resumptive clause (istinaf, a new sentence beginning). ﴿To Him I call﴾, not to other than Him. ﴿And to Him is my return﴾, meaning my return for recompense is to Him, not to other than Him. This is the matter agreed upon among the prophets. As for everything beyond that of minor branches, it varies with the eras and the nations, so there is no sense in your denying the difference in it.

(p-190) ﴿And thus﴾: like that sending down, which comprises the foundations of the religions upon which there is consensus. ﴿We sent it down as a judgment (ḥukm)﴾, judging in matters and events in accordance with what wisdom (ḥikmah) requires. ﴿In Arabic﴾: translated into the tongue of the Arabs, so that its understanding and memorization would be easy for them; and the word ﴿عَرَبِيًّا﴾ (ʿarabiyyan) is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl). ﴿And if you were to follow their desires﴾ which they call you to, such as affirming their religion and praying toward their qiblah after you have been turned away from it, ﴿after the knowledge has come to you﴾ of the abrogation (naskh) of that, ﴿you would have against God no protector and no defender﴾ who would help you and avert punishment from you. This is a cutting off of their hopes and an incitement of the believers to steadfastness in their religion.

﴿And We had already sent messengers before you﴾, humans like you. ﴿And We gave them wives and offspring﴾, women and children, just as they are for you.

﴿And it was not for a messenger﴾: it was not proper for him, nor within his power, ﴿to bring a sign﴾ that is proposed to him, or a judgment that is sought from him, ﴿except by God's permission﴾, for He is the One who has authority over that. ﴿For every term there is a Book﴾: for every time and period there is a ruling that is written for the servants according to what their welfare requires.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 13, verses 39–40:

﴿Allah erases what He wills﴾ means He abrogates (naskh) what He deems fit to abrogate. ﴿And establishes﴾ what His wisdom requires. It was also said: He erases the evil deeds of the penitent and establishes good deeds in their place. It was also said: He erases from the record of the guardian angels what carries no consequence of reward or punishment, and leaves the rest recorded, or He establishes what He alone has seen in the innermost heart. It was also said: He erases a generation and establishes others. It was also said: He erases the corrupt things that have come into being.

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read (wa-yuthabbitu) with the doubled letter (tashdid).

﴿And with Him is the Mother of the Book﴾: the origin of all books, which is the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh al-mahfuz), since there is nothing that exists except that it is written in it.

﴿And whether We show you some of what We promise them or cause you to die [before that]﴾: however the situation turns, We show you some of what We have threatened them with, or We cause you to die before it. ﴿Then upon you is only the conveyance﴾ [of the message], nothing more. ﴿And upon Us is the reckoning﴾ for recompense, not upon you. So do not concern yourself with their turning away, and do not hasten their punishment, for We will surely carry it out, and this is its vanguard.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 13, verses 41–42:

﴿Do they not see that We come to the land, reducing it from its outlying parts?﴾ The land of the disbelievers. ﴿By what We open to the Muslims from it.﴾

﴿And Allah judges; there is no repeller of His judgment.﴾ There is no one who turns it back. Its real meaning is one who nullifies a thing after it has been done (mu'aqqib, from ta'qib). From this it is said that the creditor is a mu'aqqib, because he follows his debtor, demanding repayment. The meaning is that He has decreed for Islam advancement and for disbelief retreat, and that is certain and cannot be changed. The position of "lā" together with the negated term is the accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: He judges, His judgment being executed. ﴿And He is swift in reckoning.﴾ So He will call them to account, soon, in the Hereafter, after He has punished them with killing and expulsion in this world.

﴿And those before them had already plotted.﴾ Against their prophets and the believers among them. ﴿So to Allah belongs all plotting.﴾ Since no plotting is worth regarding apart from His plotting, for He is the One able to bring about what is its intended purpose, not anyone else. ﴿He knows what every soul earns.﴾ So He prepares its recompense. ﴿And the disbelievers will know to whom belongs the good outcome of the abode.﴾ Of the two parties, wherever the punishment prepared for them comes upon them while they are heedless of it. This is in the manner of an explanation of Allah's plotting against them. The lām indicates that what is meant by "ʿuqbā" is the praiseworthy end, along with its being an idafa to "the abode," as you have understood.

Ibn Kathir, Nafi' and Abu 'Amr read ﴿al-kāfir﴾ (the disbeliever, singular) with the generic sense. It is also read ﴿al-kāfirūn﴾ (the disbelievers), ﴿alladhīna kafarū﴾ (those who disbelieved), and ﴿al-kufr﴾ (disbelief), meaning its people. ﴿And he will know who informs him when he is informed.﴾

And those who disbelieve say, "You are not a messenger." It is said that what is meant by them are the chiefs of the Jews. Say, "Sufficient is God as a witness between me and you," for He is more manifest than the proofs of my messengership, so that what is so manifest needs no other witness to testify to it. "And whoever has knowledge of the Book": this may mean the knowledge of the Qur'an and of the inimitable composition (nazm) arranged in it, or the knowledge of the Torah, which refers to Ibn Salam and those like him, or the knowledge of the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz), which is God Most High. That is, "Sufficient is the One who deserves worship, and the One who alone knows what is in the Preserved Tablet, as a witness between us, so that He will disgrace the liar among us."

This is supported by the reading of the one who reads (wa-min 'indihi) with a kasra, and (ʿilmu al-kitab) [with a damma]. According to the first reading, (ʿilm) is in the nominative as the subject of the adverbial phrase (al-zarf), since it depends on the relative pronoun. It is also permissible for it to be the subject (mubtada') with the adverbial phrase as its predicate (khabar), and on the second reading this is necessarily the case. It has also been read as (wa-min 'indihi ʿulima al-kitab), with the verb in the passive voice (al-bina' lil-maf'ul).

From the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surat al-Ra'd (the Chapter of Thunder) will be given the reward of ten good deeds for the weight of every cloud that has passed and every cloud that will come until the Day of Resurrection, and he will be raised on the Day of Resurrection among those who fulfil the covenant of God."
